analysis.one_liner: Makes the ban on internet taxes permanent and bars sales taxes on online purchases.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Commerce Committee, dying with only one cosponsor and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have taken a temporary three-year federal ban on state and local internet taxes and made it permanent, then gone further: it would have banned sales taxes on anything bought online, whether made in the U.S. or abroad. It also urged U.S. trade officials to push other countries to keep the internet free of taxes, regulation, and tariffs. The result would have been that a purchase at a local store carries sales tax while the same purchase online does not.
analysis.who_benefits: Online retailers and internet service providers gain the most: a permanent federal guarantee that they never have to collect sales taxes on online sales or pay taxes on internet access itself. Online shoppers save the sales tax on purchases, at least until states make up the lost revenue some other way.

how_it_helps.text: Makes the Internet Tax Freedom Act's three-year moratorium on state and local taxation of the internet permanent rather than expiring after three years.
Expands the ban to cover sales and use taxes on goods or services bought through electronic commerce, whether domestic or foreign.
States the Senate's position that U.S. representatives to the World Trade Organization should push for internet commerce to be free of national or local regulation, taxation, and tariffs worldwide.

analysis.who_pays: State and local governments would permanently lose sales tax revenue on a growing share of commerce — money that funds schools, police, and roads — forcing them to raise other taxes or cut services. Brick-and-mortar retailers would compete against online sellers offering the same goods tax-free. Over time, the burden would shift to taxpayers who don't buy online.
analysis.who_pays_short: State and local governments; local stores

drawbacks.text: A permanent federal ban would lock states and cities out of taxing a growing channel of commerce, eroding the sales tax base that pays for schools, police, and local services.
Exempting online sales from tax while taxing the same purchase at a local store gives online sellers a built-in price advantage over Main Street businesses.
The bill would push a blanket no-tax, no-regulation position on electronic commerce internationally, foreclosing future policy choices rather than weighing them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Online shoppers and internet sellers get a real, immediate benefit: no sales tax and no access taxes, permanently. But the cost is structural — a shrinking state and local tax base and an uneven playing field against local stores. Since online buying was growing fast in 1999, a permanent exemption (rather than a temporary freeze while policymakers studied the issue) would have locked in a large and expanding revenue loss for governments that fund everyday public services.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced by Senator McCain in September 1999 and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, it was never taken up and expired when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 22, 1999, with Majority Leader Trent Lott introducing it on Senator McCain's behalf, and was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
It would have made the three-year moratorium on state and local internet taxation permanent and extended it to sales and use taxes on goods bought online.
It attracted only one cosponsor, a Republican.
No further action was taken — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State and local governments and brick-and-mortar retailers are better off because the bill died: they kept the existing tax treatment and the temporary moratorium was never made permanent. Online retailers did not get the guaranteed permanent exemption they would have gained.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: State and local governments; Main Street retailers

for.name: Sen. John McCain
for.role: U.S. Senator (R-AZ); bill sponsor and chairman of the Senate Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to make the internet tax moratorium permanent and bar sales taxes on e-commerce.

for.name: Sen. Trent Lott
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on Senator McCain's behalf.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never reported it out; no hearing, markup, or vote ever occurred.

against.name: State and local governments
against.role: Governors, mayors, and tax administrators nationwide
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed making the internet tax moratorium permanent, arguing it would erode state and local sales tax revenue.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so no party split was recorded; the bill had a Republican sponsor and a single Republican cosponsor and died in committee.

industries.note: A permanent exemption from sales taxes on online purchases gives internet sellers a built-in price advantage over local stores and permanently removes a growing revenue stream from state and local governments, shifting costs to other taxpayers.
Making the Internet Tax Freedom Act moratorium permanent protects ISPs from state and local taxes on internet access, a cost that would otherwise tend to be passed on to internet users.
The bill permanently bars them from collecting sales tax on electronic commerce, shrinking the revenue that funds schools, police, and local services.
They would keep collecting sales tax while online competitors selling identical goods would not, creating a permanent price disadvantage for local stores.
